title: Elijah Nicolas’ 2003 Porsche 911 Marks Milestones

body_markdown:
In 2003, Porsche built 1963 examples of a special-edition, highly optioned 911 to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the model. At that time, I was finishing up my degree and generally figuring out what I wanted to do with my life. Two things were certain: I was done pursuing medicine, and I was going to fulfill my childhood dream of owning a Porsche 911.


Over the next 18 years, I eschewed med school for flight school, became a commercial pilot, got married, had kids, bought a house, and parked everything from Mercedes-AMGs to Toyota Priuses in my garage. I had built a life I was proud of, but still, no Porsche.


All the while, prices were steadily rising, and I watched the various windows of affordability for the different generations of 911s shrink while I saved. My initial target of $25,000–$30,000 had come and gone, so I came up with a new number: I would own a 911 before I turned 40. Everything went according to plan—barely. I bought this[2003 Porsche 911](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/2003/2003-porsche-911-carrera?id=aCn1I000000CxUWSA0) 40 Jahre (German for “40 Years”) a few weeks ahead of my 40th birthday.


Fun fact: Nicolas’ Porsche marks the first time Hagerty has had **3 million cars** with active policies! Hagerty was founded in 1984 in Traverse City, Michigan, where our headquarters remain.


James Lipman


I’ve owned #310/1963 for about five years now, and the significance behind the model hasn’t been lost on me in that time. For any lifelong fan of the brand, parking a piece of Porsche history in your garage is a privilege, but this machine’s meaning is far more personal: It represents my past, present, and future.


As is surely the case for many of my fellow[Hagerty Drivers Club members](https://www.hagerty.com/media/category/member-stories/) , my love for cars coincides with my earliest memories—specifically, going for rides in and taking photos on an old 35mm camera of my uncle’s[1985 Toyota Supra](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/this-1985-toyota-supra-is-a-dream-come-true-for-10-year-old-me/) (shoutout to all the Cool Uncles with fun cars out there, you play an important part in perpetuating enthusiast car culture!).


I’ve been enamored with cars and photography ever since, but there were plenty of other formative moments along the way, including my first time “driving” as a 7-year-old perched on my father’s lap, steering our family’s 1977 Dodge Tradesman 200 van on a road trip between my native San Diego and Los Angeles. I am still proud of the fact that I only hit the little reflector bumps between the freeway lanes three times over the course of this adventure.


Later, when I was officially licensed to drive, I took possession of my first car, a 1985 Mercedes-Benz 300D passed down from my parents. A slow turbodiesel sedan is hardly a 16-year-old boy’s dream, but I loved that car for what it meant to my family. Both of my parents had emigrated from the Philippines before meeting and marrying in the States, and their American Dream was never going to be complete without a Benz in the garage. We drove it everywhere when I was growing up (I particularly enjoyed sitting on the fold-down center armrest in the back seat).


In 1997, Porsche unveiled the fifth generation of the 911, commonly referred to as the 996. It marked a massive change for the 911 lineage, which had theretofore evolved in slow, steady increments. Unlike every prior generation of the 911, this one had a water- rather than air-cooled engine. If that wasn’t enough to make the purists cry sacrilege, one needed only to look at the shape of the headlights, which remain a source of controversy. I, however, loved everything about it.


To me, it was the perfect cutting-edge update to the venerated 911. It was tech-forward, fresh-looking but still familiar, and thus the 996 became my proverbial poster car. It took almost two decades before I called one my own.


I joke that I commute for a living, and what better way to pass the time with copilots than chat about shared interests? Unsurprisingly, many of those drawn to flying also appreciate driving. One captain’s prized possession was an[E28-generation BMW 5 Series](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/low-miles-big-price-for-record-breaking-196k-bmw-e28-m5/) . I recall another who rebuilt his Ferrari 308 from the ground up to concours condition. That was all well and good, but one of my colleagues’ car histories really stood out to me. This guy had owned 12 different 911s, but he ultimately kept just two, one being a 40 Jahre.


Porsche built 1963 special 911s to mark the car’s 40th anniversary. All featured dark gray leather.


James Lipman


We stayed in touch, during which time I became ready to purchase my first 911. I still wanted a 996-generation 911, and the more I learned about the 40 Jahre version, the more my mind was made up. I didn’t want the additional costs and complexities of a Turbo model, nor the aggression of a[GT3](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/porsche-911-gt3-six-generations-of-flat-six-glory/) , but a regular run-of-the-mill 911 wouldn’t quite cut it, either.


> To me, the 996 was the perfect cutting-edge update to the 911.


Besides the anniversary element, you are probably wondering what makes a 40 Jahre unique, right? It comes with the Porsche X51 Powerkit for the flat-six engine, which features higher-flow intake and exhaust manifolds, revised camshafts, high-lift valves, software tweaks, and other modifications to up the performance from the base model. Besides the additional horsepower from the Powerkit, the 40 Jahre cars also featured polished lightweight wheels, a front bumper cover borrowed from the Porsche Turbo, a standard limited-slip differential, sportier suspension, and GT Silver exterior paint (the same color that the Carrera GT supercar debuted with), among a long list of creature comforts from the 911 option book.


They wore GT Silver metallic paint and came standard with a sunroof.


James Lipman


Other touches included polished aluminium wheels and polished tailpipes.


James Lipman


I found a good one for sale in Arizona and told my wife we were taking a flight to Phoenix to “look at a car.” I’m not sure if she realized we’d be driving it home, but I know we had an unforgettable voyage on our way home. I’ll never forget those first few on-ramp pulls or going through the gears as we wove through the Sierra Nevada, the sun setting ahead of us. It was a sublime trip, and worth the wait.


This 911 is the culmination of my childhood interests and the realization of long-term planning. One day, I’ll teach my three children how to drive a manual in it. I look forward to those full-circle moments (but I’m in no rush). The dream was always a 911. What I didn’t know back then is that the best part of owning one would be whom I get to give it to.


James Lipman
